newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss say claims they hid Nazi wealth unverified.
newsitem.headline: Swiss say claims they hid Nazi wealth unverified.

text.p: Swiss diplomatic envoy Thomas Borer hit back at U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato on Thursday, saying the American politician had used unverified documents to accuse Switzerland of having helped Nazis to conceal their wealth.

Borer has emerged as his country's primary spokesman on the issue after being named by Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti in October to head a task force charged with countering a wave of negative publicity abroad.
He said he regretted that D'Amato had continued to attack Switzerland on the basis of individual documents from U.S. World War Two archives which had not been counter-checked by historians.

D'Amato, a New York Republican, released a State Department report on Wednesday that he said raised suspicions that German Nazis routinely used Swiss diplomatic pouches to send looted wealth secretly to Argentina during the Second World War.

Berne, faced with a drumbeat of accusations that Switzerland profited cynically from both Nazis and their Jewish victims, has asked D'Amato and other critics to tone down their attacks while three separate Swiss probes run their course.

"What I once again regret is that Mr D'Amato is presenting obvious allegations as proven facts and basing himself solely on sources that have not be checked," Borer, who is deputy secretary general in the foreign ministry, told Reuters.
"Serious historical research requires that statements in one source be checked against independent sources," he added.

Borer, 39, was counsellor for legal and political affairs at the Swiss embassy in Washington in 1993-94. He has been assigned to counter the bad publicity Switzerland has drawn over claims Swiss banks helped Nazis hide stolen loot and sat on unclaimed assets belonging to Jews who perished in the Holocaust.
Borer said D'Amato had still not replied to a month-old offer to meet personally.

"My offer still stands. I have let him know I will be in Washington (D.C.) next week," he said. Borer is due to testify on December 11 at a House Banking Committee hearing on war-time Swiss banking and Swiss gold purchases from Nazi Germany.

Borer was also expected to meet officials at the U.S. State Department, which is probing the fate of Nazi assets, and the World Jewish Congress in New York, which has pressured Swiss banks into a search for lost accounts left by Holocaust victims.
"My priority next week will be to make Switzerland's position clear in the United States," he said.
Berne and Swiss banks say they are committed to scrutinising their war-time financial past and will redress any wrongs that come to light, but only based on serious and solid research.

Borer said he had never before heard accusations of the sort now raised by D'Amato that Swiss bankers entrusted with government diplomatic pouches during the war years may have used them to sneak Nazi wealth into Argentina.
"I cannot confirm or deny that. This is a question for historical enquiry," Borer said.
"But there is the question of why the Allies did not intervene sharply with Switzerland if in 1946 or 1947 they knew this to be a fact rather than an allegation," he added.

Borer said D'Amato's latest accusations would be one of the subjects for study by a commission of independent historians and other experts proposed by the Swiss government and expected to win final approval from parliament next week.
The enquiry will be a broad review of Swiss financial relations with Nazi Germany and the fate of wealth that poured into neutral Switzerland from Nazis as well as their victims.
Swiss banks and Jewish groups are running a separate probe focused just on the fate of dormant accounts.
